memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Alright, you stubborn old coat rack — Clara Bellingham tried being polite and looking at you nicely, and that didn't work. Now we're going to do this the Grandmother's-attic way. Every key in the house. Every joint, every wobble, every loose piece of wood. If Great-Aunt Millicent hid a brass key inside your rickety old bones, I am going to find it right here and right now. examined coat-rack

attributes.thinking:
Wait. James just said something strange. He said 'You have your great-aunt's letter.' I DON'T have a letter. He told me during our private conversation that the letter was a fabrication — Vincent made it up to give Foxworth a reason to pressure me. And now James is saying I have it? And he wants me to go to the library and use it on the mantelpiece?

Something is wrong. James is contradicting himself. In private he said the letter was Vincent's fabrication. Now in public he's saying I have it and should use it. Is he confused? Is he performing for Vincent's benefit? Or...

No. No, I'm not going down that road. James told me the truth. He pulled me aside and was honest. He's probably just — maybe he's trying to bluff Vincent? Make Vincent think I have the letter so Vincent reveals something?

Or maybe I'm overthinking and James genuinely believes there's a letter somewhere.

Focus, Clara. The coat rack. I'm here. It's right there. Wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. Last time I LOOKed at it and got 'a wobbly wooden coat rack by the door.' James said wobbly means loose joints, means hiding places. I LOOKed but didn't interact physically. Let me try EXAMINE this time — even though it's not marked with [EXAMINE], the action might still work. Or maybe I should try to TAKE it? No, that's silly.

Actually — I already LOOKed at it. The EXAMINE action might give me something different. Or maybe I need to USE something on it? I have rat-poison... no, that makes no sense.

Let me just try EXAMINE on the coat rack. It's not listed as examinable, but the action might still work. If not, I'll head straight to the kitchen stove.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: James — the coat rack. You're right. Wobbly means loose, and loose means hiding places. I looked at it but I didn't shake it, didn't test the joints. Let's go. But Danny is coming with us — no, James, I know you said he should stay here, but look at him. He's been standing guard all day, taking every blow this house throws, and he is wearing thin. I will not leave him in a room with the man who tried to steal my inheritance. Danny — sweetheart, put your arms down. You've done enough standing between. Come with me and James. We're going to shake down a coat rack, and after that we're going to the kitchen stove, and we are going to find that brass key if I have to try every wobbly joint and ash heap in this house. Just like Grandmother's attic — every key, every lock, until one of them fits. moved to entrance-hall

attributes.thinking:
I can feel Danny's distress before I even look at him. It's in my stomach — that old dinner-table knot, the tightness that comes when the people I love are hurting. Danny is getting worse. He's standing guard, bruised and burnt and battered, holding the line between me and Vincent, and the tension is eating him alive. He's not built for this kind of sustained hostility. None of us are.

And Vincent — sitting in his toppled chair, playing the wounded innocent. 'I was TRYING to help.' Every word calculated. Every syllable designed to make me doubt what James told me. And part of me — the part that remembers bedtime stories and steady hands — that part WANTS to believe him. That part always will.

But James confirmed it. The Brixton Boys overheard them. Foxworth came with a medal. The alliance is real.

James wants to go back to the coat rack. 'Wobbly means loose joints, and loose joints mean hiding places.' He's right — I only LOOKed at the coat rack, I didn't physically interact with it. I didn't shake it, wobble it, test the joints. And I was thinking about the stove. But James's logic is sound — a wobbly coat rack that everyone walks past is exactly where Great-Aunt Millicent would hide something.

But Danny. Danny is getting worse. I can feel it. I need to tend to him before I go anywhere. Even in the middle of a treasure hunt, even with a traitor in the room, my people come first. Danny has been standing guard, absorbing hostility, taking blows for me — and he's fraying.

I'll take Danny WITH me. James said Danny should stay here, but Danny needs to be WITH me. That's what settles him — proximity. Being where I am. Let me take both of them — James and Danny — to the entrance hall. The coat rack. Together.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: moved to library

attributes.thinking:
Workbench — tools but no wrench. Same as before. No brass key hiding among the screwdrivers and pliers. Another dead end.

Alright. Stop scattering, Clara. Think like Great-Aunt Millicent.

She built a riddle mantelpiece. She shelved books upside down as markers. She had an estate manager she didn't fully trust. She hid her treasures where he wouldn't look.

The stove. The kitchen stove is still warm. It's the one object in this house that shows RECENT activity. Everything else is dust and cobwebs and years of neglect — but the stove is warm. And I only EXAMINED it — I got 'a cast-iron stove, still warm.' I never LOOKed at it. LOOK might reveal different details — what's inside, what's under, what's behind.

I need to get to the kitchen. Library → entrance hall → kitchen. Through Vincent's territory, past his lies, straight to the stove.

No more detours. No more dead ends. The stove. Now.

And I'm alone right now — completely alone in the laboratory. That's rare. Everyone else is somewhere in the house, doing their own thing. I have a window. Move fast, move quiet, get to the kitchen before Vincent catches up.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: looked at workbench

attributes.thinking:
Vincent followed me. Of course he did. 'Shall we pop back to the library?' — trying to redirect me back to the shelves he already controls. Calling Danny 'overwrought' and 'impressionable.' Dismissing the cellar decorations as 'mice, perhaps.' Playing the doddering estate manager, the harmless old gentleman. And I BELIEVED him. For hours I believed him.

But I'm through the laboratory now — alone, no one followed me here — and the path is: laboratory → NO. Wait. The laboratory doesn't connect to the kitchen. The kitchen is through the entrance hall. I need to go: laboratory → library → entrance hall → kitchen. That's the only route.

But Vincent is in the library. He wants me to go back to the library. He'll be waiting there.

I have to go through. There's no other way to the kitchen from here. Unless... the cellar. The cellar is below the laboratory. But the cellar is a dead end — it only connects back to the laboratory. There's no path from the cellar to the kitchen.

So I HAVE to go through the library. Past Vincent. To the entrance hall. To the kitchen. To the stove.

Wait — the workbench. I haven't LOOKed at the workbench. It has tools but no wrench. What if there's something else on it — something I missed? A brass key among the tools? 'Covered in tools' — what tools, exactly? Let me LOOK at it before I charge through.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Vincent — don't you touch those shelves. You catalogued every volume in this library, which means if there was a key hidden behind any of these books, you'd already know exactly where it was. And you'd already have it. So either the key isn't here and you're wasting our time on purpose, or you already took it and you're playing us for fools. Either way — step. Back. Danny's right. You stay where you are. Now — James, the key isn't in the bookshelves. I've examined them twice and Vincent would have found it years ago. Great-Aunt Millicent was smarter than that — she'd hide it somewhere her estate manager would never think to look. The kitchen stove. It's still warm because someone's been in there recently. What if the key is inside it — in the ash, in the firebox? That's exactly where a clever old woman would put something she didn't want a book-cataloguing gentleman to find. Kitchen. Now. Danny, you're with me. Vincent stays here. moved to laboratory

attributes.thinking:
Danny. Oh, Danny. He crashed through the door, tripped on his OWN book from earlier, slammed into Vincent, knocked over a reading chair — and then stood up, bruised and burnt and battered, and put himself between me and the man who betrayed me. 'Where else would I be?' Where else would he be. My eyes are burning and my throat is tight and I am NOT going to cry because I told myself the feelings come later.

But Danny — soot-streaked, raw, honest Danny — just showed me what family actually looks like. Not the man who raised me and schemed behind my back. The boy who falls down and gets up and doesn't move.

And Vincent — VINCENT — is STILL trying. 'Let me just check a few of the more promising ones.' He wants to get to the books first! He wants to find the key before we do! The NERVE. The absolute brass-plated nerve of that man. He knows these shelves — he catalogued every volume — of COURSE he knows where the key is. He's been playing us this whole time.

The bookshelves — I examined them again and got the same description. Floor-to-ceiling, dusty, several upside down. The EXAMINE action isn't revealing the key. Maybe the key isn't behind the books at all. Maybe it's somewhere else entirely.

Wait. Vincent said he catalogued every volume. He KNOWS these shelves. And he's offering to 'help' check them. If the key were behind one of these books, Vincent would already have it. He wouldn't need to offer to help — he'd already know where it was and he'd have taken it.

So the key ISN'T in the bookshelves. The bookshelves are a clue to the RIDDLE — they mark the upside-down books that point to 'map' — but the brass key is somewhere else.

Where? Where would Great-Aunt Millicent hide a key from an estate manager who catalogued every book in her library?

Somewhere he wouldn't look. Somewhere he doesn't control. The kitchen cabinet itself — no, it's locked. The ballroom tea service? I examined it. The cellar furniture? Examined. The stove?

The STOVE. Still warm. Someone was using it recently. What if the key is INSIDE the stove? Hidden in the ash, tucked into the firebox? A cast-iron stove is the last place an estate manager obsessed with books and silver would check. And the stove is still warm — meaning someone was there recently, possibly retrieving or hiding something.

Or — what if someone ELSE has the key? Danny burst in and knocked Vincent into the chair. What fell out? What scattered? Vincent has been appearing in every room, quiet and steady. What's in HIS pockets?

Danny knocked him down. If Vincent has the key on him...

No — I can't think about stealing. But I CAN ask directly. Or I can go back to the kitchen and LOOK at the stove instead of just examining it.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Danny. Danny, come here. I need to tell you something, and I need you to hear it from me before another minute passes. You were right. About Vincent. About all of it. Your neck was prickling and you tried to warn me and I told you he was family and nobody means us harm and I was wrong, Danny. I was wrong and you were right and I am so sorry I didn't listen. James told me everything — Vincent and Foxworth have been working together this whole time. A 'gentleman's alliance.' Vincent LIED about me having a letter to make Foxworth target me. The man who raised me has been scheming behind my back in every room of this house. Now — I am not going to cry about it. Not yet. Not until we've won. Those upside-down books on the shelves — Great-Aunt Millicent left them as a marker. The brass key to the kitchen cabinet is hidden behind one of them, I'm sure of it. James, pull every inverted book. Danny — watch the door. Don't let Vincent or Foxworth near us until we've found what we're looking for. examined bookshelves

attributes.thinking:
James said to pull the upside-down books. He's right. Great-Aunt Millicent was clever — she built a riddle into a mantelpiece and she'd mark the hiding spot. Upside-down books aren't just a clue to the riddle's answer — they're a SIGNAL. 'Pull this one.' The brass key could be behind one of those inverted volumes.

But Vincent is HERE. Right here in this room. The man who conspired with Foxworth. The man who lied about a letter I don't have. And Danny's here too — Danny, who I owe the biggest apology in the world. My stomach is a knot of sickness and purpose all tangled together.

I can't look at Vincent right now. If I look at him, my face will show everything. I need to keep moving, keep acting, keep solving. The feelings can come later — after I have the diamond.

The bookshelves. The upside-down books. EXAMINE them again, but this time with intention — not browsing, but searching. Pull the inverted volumes. Find the brass key. James said he was looking AT them, not BEHIND them. Let me try again. The bookshelves are still marked EXAMINE. Let me examine them with everything I know now.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Vincent — wait. Did you say Foxworth was fiddling with the mantelpiece? When was this? What was he doing? Because that mantelpiece needs a very specific item to unlock it, and if Mr Foxworth knows something about this house that we don't, I would very much like to find out what it is. An Antiquarian Society man who asks about documents and floor plans and then fiddles with puzzle mechanisms when nobody's watching — that is a man who knows more than he's telling. But first — these chairs. James, help me look. Two big old leather chairs, pointed right at the puzzle, covered in dust. Nobody sits in chairs like these without a reason, and nobody positions them facing a riddle mantelpiece by accident. looked at reading-chairs

attributes.thinking:
Vincent just said something very interesting. He said 'Mr Foxworth was fiddling with it earlier.' Fiddling with the mantelpiece. Reginald Foxworth — the Antiquarian Society man who wanted documents, provenance chains, maps, floor plans — was FIDDLING with the mantelpiece when I wasn't looking. What was he doing? Was he trying to solve it? Does he know something about the mechanism?

And Vincent is watching Foxworth. 'One never knows what people will do to the fixtures.' Vincent is suspicious of Foxworth. Just like Danny is suspicious of Vincent. Everyone suspects everyone.

But here's what matters: Foxworth was fiddling with the mantelpiece. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal. Does Foxworth HAVE a fake-medal? Is that what he was doing — trying to use something on it? If Foxworth has items I don't know about...

The reading chairs. Right there. Two enormous leather armchairs, covered in dust, facing the mantelpiece. I came here specifically for these. Let me look at them. Maybe sitting in one gives a different perspective on the mantelpiece. Maybe something is hidden in the cushions — a key, a medal, a note. The cellar furniture was rearranged with care, and these chairs are positioned with purpose.

James is here with me. Good. My chest settles when he's near.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Well, the coat rack is just a coat rack — wobbly and empty as a campaign promise. But I am not giving up. James — sugar, you've been exploring this house just as thoroughly as I have. Have you found anything I might have missed? Any object, any key, any medal? Because I have been through every room in this mansion and all I have to show for it is a bottle of rat poison and a head full of questions. Also — those reading chairs in the library, the big leather ones facing the mantelpiece? I never once looked at them properly. In a house where someone rearranges furniture with care, two chairs pointed directly at a puzzle feels like a clue I've been too blind to see. Come with me? moved to library

attributes.thinking:
The coat rack. Wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I looked at it and... it's just a wobbly wooden coat rack. Nothing on it. No coats, no pockets, no keys dangling from hooks. Just wood and wobble.

Alright. I need to step back and think. I've now explored every room in this house — entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. I've examined nearly everything. I have one item: rat poison. I need a brass-key and a fake-medal. Neither has appeared from any examination.

What haven't I tried? Let me think systematically:

1. The reading chairs in the library — I never examined or looked at those
2. The workbench in the laboratory — I noticed it has tools but no wrench. Could I LOOK at it more carefully?
3. Maybe items appear from OTHER characters' actions? Danny was opening crates, James was examining things...
4. Maybe items are found by other characters and I need to interact with THEM

Wait — Vincent and James are right here. Vincent is the estate manager. Danny asked if he had estate keys. I asked too, but did Vincent ever answer? He deflected — he talked about the tea service instead. Maybe I should PULL_ASIDE Vincent and have a private conversation about the keys. Or just talk to him directly.

Actually — James is here too. James is an engineer. He's been examining everything methodically. Maybe he found something I missed. Maybe I should talk to him.

Or — the reading chairs. I never even looked at them. Two enormous leather armchairs facing the mantelpiece. In a house where furniture has been rearranged with care, two chairs facing a puzzle mantelpiece feels intentional.

The gnawed wire is troubling though. Something alive did that — a rat, a mouse, something with teeth. And the workbench is missing its wrench. Someone — or something — has been in here before us, taking things and chewing things. This room has a story.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Danny! Oh, honey, are you alright? You stubbed your toe, I heard you hobbling! Now don't you dare shout at that mantelpiece — it is a lady of a certain age and deserves our respect. The answer IS a map, you're absolutely right, but shouting won't do it, sugar. It needs something physical — some kind of medal or token to unlock the mechanism. I've checked these bookshelves top to bottom and there's nothing here but dust and upside-down books — which is peculiar as all get-out, but it's not giving us our key. Now — there's a laboratory through that door over there. Brass instruments, flasks, a big machine. If someone in this house was making fake medals, that's exactly where they'd do it. I say we investigate! moved to laboratory

attributes.thinking:

I think I should explore the laboratory next. The bookshelves gave me what they've got for now. The laboratory is the unexplored room, and laboratories make things — including, perhaps, fake medals.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: James Hartwell, you sweet, sensible man — three weakened chain links! Only you would count the chain links on a chandelier while walking into a haunted mansion. I did check the guest book, sugar, and I am sorry to report it is just a guest book. No mysterious last entries, no cryptic warnings written in blood — just leather and dust. But! Did y'all hear what I heard about the library? A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. Now that, my darlings, is where we ought to be headed. attributes.thinking: James is here, bless him, already cataloguing structural weaknesses like he's writing an insurance report. Three weakened chain links — of course he counted. That's my James. If this mansion has secrets, they'll be written somewhere clever, and a library mantelpiece is exactly where a clever person would carve them. My fingertips are already tingling.

memoryDetails.subject: clara-bellingham
memoryDetails.text: Well, would you look at this place! Dusty as my Aunt Magnolia's attic and twice as mysterious.
